h: Chips, sweets and the eras you might miss
p: Beamish has grown a lot over the years, and it's easy to stick to the famous 1900s town and miss some of the best bits. Out at Pockerley you'll find an older manor house and a waggonway telling the story of the early days of railways, with replica steam locomotives from the age of George Stephenson. The farm is set in the 1940s, a nice reminder of wartime rationing and Land Girls, and newer areas have been opening to show the North East through the 1950s, a real nostalgia hit for grandparents.

Now, the food. The fried fish and chip shop in the pit village cooks its chips the old way, in beef dripping over coal-fired ranges, and the queue tells you how popular it is, so eat early or late to dodge the lunchtime rush. Down in the town, the sweet shop makes traditional boiled sweets, and watching the sugar being pulled and cut is a highlight for kids and adults alike. The bakery and the pub are both worth a nose too.

Think about your route. The trams and buses connect everything, but they get busy, so walking between nearby areas can be quicker. Grab a map at the entrance, pick the areas that matter most to your group and treat the rest as a bonus.

If you're staying around, the Tanfield Railway near Stanley claims a very long history and runs steam trains on certain days, and Durham city's cathedral and riverside walks are an easy run down the road. Gateshead's Angel of the North is close by for a quick photo stop on the way home.
